Upper Extremity Neuropathy

Etiology and Pathophysiology ❑Neuropathy= Injury along the pathway of the nerve, often peripheral nerve • Can be result of compression/tension, transection, issue with blood supply, inflammation, degeneration, metabolic disease, or radiation induced ❑3 types of nerve injuries 1.Neuropraxia= mild injury, affects the myelin 2. Axonotomesis= more significant, breakdown of myelin + nerve axon but surrounding connective tissue intact→ Wallerian degeneration • axonal regrowth occurs 3.Neurotomesis= most severe, breakdown of myelin + nerve axon + surrounding connective tissue • No chance of regrowth

Principles Of Patient Presentation ❑Complaints of sensory disturbances in the distribution of the nerve ❑Sharp/piercing pain ❑Tingling/Dysesthesia ❑Numbness ❑Exacerbation of symptoms may occur with activity or specific positioning ❑Percussion or pain in distribution of the nerve will often be an examination finding ❑Tinel’s sign
Dermatomes and Peripheral Nerve Sensory Distribution

Testing ❑Can be diagnosed clinically, but most effective measure → nerve conduction studies (NCS) and electromyography (EMG) ❑NCS looks at nerve signal speed using surface electrodes and delivering shock ❑EMG involves inserting tiny needle into muscle to examine electrical activity with contraction ❑Both assist to distinguishing injury and grading severity and chronicity ❑Imaging can assist in evaluation of sources of compression ❑Ultrasound has expanding role due to multiple benefits ❑Evaluation of multiple possible sources of compression (soft tissue, fluid, bone) ❑Visual indicators of compression ❑Dynamic assessment
Carpal tunnel on Ultrasound

Suprascapular Nerve ❑Nerve: Mixed nerve innervating Supraspinatus and Infraspinatus and sensory of GH and AC joint ❑Compression: Result of trauma, cyst, or fracture ❑Sites of compression ❑ suprascapular notch ❑ spinoglenoid notch
Suprascapular Nerve Continued ❑Management ❑Physical therapy ❑OMT and manual therapy ❑Injections: Nerve Hydrodissections vs Nerve blocks ❑Surgery: surgical release

Axillary Nerve ❑Nerve: mixed nerve innervating Deltoid and teres minor and sensation over lateral shoulder ❑Compression: trauma (fracture or dislocation), positioning, muscle hypertrophy or cyst formation ❑MCC (most common cause)= trauma ❑Treatment ❑Physical therapy and OMT ❑Surgery: nerve grafting

Musculocutaneous Nerve Nerve: mixed nerve innervating coracobrachialis, biceps, and brachialis and becomes lateral cutaneous nerve → sensation of lateral forearm Compression: shoulder dislocation, strenuous exercise, malpositioning during anesthesia Treatment: Mostly conservative care including PT and topical medications

Dorsal Scapular Nerve ❑Mostly motor innervating rhomboid muscles and levator scapulae with some sensory to scapula ❑Compression: muscle hypertrophy/spasm or microtrauma ❑Present with pain along medial border or scapula or contribute to winging of scapula ❑Treatment: Physical therapy, OMT, Injections 16

Median Nerve ❑MC entrapment neuropathy of the upper extremity ❑Nerve: Mixed nerve with sensation of thenar eminence (palmar cutaneous nerve branch) and digits 1-3 and radial half of digit 4 ❑Branches off for motor→ anterior interosseous nerve innervating muscles of the hand (FPL, FDP 2 and 3) ❑Injury: Overuse, Trauma, Pregnancy, amyloidosis, Autoimmune disorders, Cyst formation ❑Multiple areas of compression → breakdown of proximal or distal median nerve entrapment

Proximal Median Nerve Entrapment ❑Pronator Teres syndrome- entrapment beneath pronator teres → sensory loss of thenar eminence + digits 1-3 and pain with pronation ❑Ligament of Struthers- compression underneath ligament by medial epicondyle ❑Presentation like Pronator teres, with compression more proximal → weakness in pronation ❑Anterior interosseous syndrome- compression in forearm compartment → only motor findings with inability to form “O” with thumb and forefinger

Distal Median Nerve Entrapment ❑Carpal Tunnel syndrome- MCC of median neuropathy caused by entrapment under the flexor retinaculum → sensory findings in first 3 fingers and lateral aspect of 4th finger ❑Symptoms normally worse at night ❑Physical examination: provocative tests (Tinel’s sign, Phalen’s test, Reverse Phalen’s test) ❑Most specific finding= positive flick sign

Median Neuropathy Treatment ❑Important to localize lesion and understand source of compression ❑Treatment starts conservative care ❑Physical therapy/Occupational therapy ❑Wrist splint- night time use ❑OMT ❑Topical Analgesics + Anti-inflammatories ❑Interventional Procedures ❑Injections ❑Thread Release ❑Surgery- Transverse carpal ligament release

Ulnar Nerve Entrapment ❑Nerve: mixed nerve innervating intrinsic hand muscles and palmar + dorsal sensation of digits 4 and 5 ❑Compression: MC at the elbow (cubital tunnel) or at the wrist (Guyon’s canal ❑Causes= valgus deformity, prolonged positioning/resting, anatomical variants ❑Physical Examination: Sensory or intrinsic muscle deficits ❑Treatment: Focused on behavioral modification or mechanical adjustments ❑Does not respond well to injections or Physical therapy ❑Refractory cases → surgery for decompression
Ulnar Nerve Pathway

Radial Nerve Entrapment ❑Nerve: Mixed motor and sensory innervating triceps, brachioradialis, wrist/finger extensors and sensory to dorsal aspect of digits 1-3 + lateral aspect of digit 4. ❑Compression: Trauma (fracture), prolonged positioning, microtrauma ❑Spiral groove → wrist drop and decreased sensation of the dorsum of hand and digits 1-3 ❑Proximal forearm affecting Posterior Interosseous Nerve → wrist drop without affecting ECRL and supination ❑Treatment: Mostly responds to conservative therapy focused on elimination of aggravating factor
Lower Extremity Neuropathy

Superior Cluneal Nerve ❑Nerve: Sensory nerve providing sensation to upper portion of buttocks inferior to iliac crest ❑Compression: microtrauma or muscle hypertrophy/spasm ❑Presentation hallmark of pain along the iliac crest with radiation into the buttocks region ❑Treatment: Not as responsive to conservative measures ❑US guided injections or radiofrequency ablation

Sciatic Nerve ❑Nerve: Mixed motor and sensory nerve innervating posterior thigh muscles and giving branches (tibial and common peroneal nerves) to lower leg and foot and sensory of posterior leg and foot ❑Compression: direct trauma, muscle hypertrophy/tightness, iatrogenic (surgery), irritation from scar tissue/bone spur ❑Can have similar presentation to common peroneal neuropathy (discussed later) ❑Treatment: Mostly focused on eliminating compressive cause, and often responds very well to physical therapy and OMT/manual therapy ❑Presence of foot drop at initial evaluation is a sign of poor prognosis
Sciatic Nerve anatomy

Differential diagnosis PIRIFORMIS SYNDROME ❑Buttock pain with walking ❑Pain worse after sitting for prolonged period of time ❑Referral of pain down the thigh to the knee ❑Decreased Internal rotation and pain with internal rotation (FAIR test) or hip preference for external rotation HAMSTRING SYNDROME ❑Result of prior hamstring injury ❑Common in runners, sprinters, or explosive sport athletes ❑Triad 1. Increased Pain with sitting 2. Pain with resist knee flexion at 90 degrees hip flexion 3. Pain on palpation of ischial tuberosity

Differential Treatment PIRIFORMIS SYNDROME ❑Physical therapy ❑Emphasis on stretching and strengthening surrounding hip abductor and external rotator muscles ❑OMT ❑Injections ❑Surgery to release piriformis muscle HAMSTRING SYNDROME ❑Physical therapy ❑Emphasis on gradual increase in loading hamstring muscles ❑OMT ❑Activity modification- using wedge cushion when sitting ❑Injections ❑Surgery to fix hamstring tear
Hamstring Syndrome

Obturator Nerve ❑Nerve: Mixed nerve innervating hip adductor muscles and sensory for medial thigh ❑Compression: pelvic trauma, surgery, mass, or inflammation from osteitis pubis ❑Treatment: Often delay in diagnosis until muscle changes begin to occur from motor involvement ❑Surgery and physical therapy

Femoral Nerve ❑Nerve: Mixed nerve innervating the anterior thigh muscles and sensory to anterior thigh + medial part of lower leg and foot ❑Compression: trauma during surgery or childbirth, pelvic masses or bleeding ❑Presentation often occurs with knee extension/hip flexion weakness more than sensory changes ❑Treatment: Favorable prognosis that responds well to PT ❑Surgery with nerve grafting needed in direct traumatic injury

Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve ❑Nerve: Sensory nerve responsible for sensation of anterolateral thigh ❑Compression: beneath inguinal ligament due to body habitus, tight fitting clothes, heavy belts, or iatrogenic injury during surgery ❑Most cases result in normal findings on EMG ❑Treatment: Emphasis on weight loss or avoidance of external pressure ❑OMT and local anesthetics injections can be beneficial in refractory cases
Meralgia Paresthetica

Tibial Nerve ❑Nerve: Mixed motor and sensory nerve innervating muscles of plantar flexion, inversion, and flexion of toes and sensory to plantar part of foot ❑Becomes posterior tibial nerve as it enters tarsal tunnel ❑Compression: Multiple areas of entrapment with different etiologies ❑Tarsal tunnel (MC): Fracture/dislocation, tendinopathy, microtrauma, scar tissue formation ❑Medial Plantar nerve: tendinopathy, microtrauma (overpronation), prior surgery, cyst formation ❑Lateral Plantar Nerve (Baxter’s nerve): poor foot biomechanics, anatomical abnormalities, chronic inflammation

Tibial Nerve Entrapment Treatment ❑Rarely do patients present with motor weakness ❑Most cases responds to conservative measures ❑ PT ❑OMT ❑Shoe modifications ❑Orthotics ❑Topical medications ❑ Injections can be done if failing conservative measures ❑Less frequently utilized due to difficulty of localizing on ultrasound ❑Surgery: considered after failed conservative treatment >3 months ❑Best outcomes if compression source was ganglionic cyst

Common Peroneal (fibular) Nerve ❑Nerve: Mixed motor and sensory nerve that innervates short head of biceps femoris and wraps around fibular head and branches → superficial and deep peroneal nerves ❑Superficial peroneal nerve: innervates peroneal muscles and sensation to majority of the dorsum of foot* ❑Deep peroneal nerve: innervates muscle responsible for dorsiflexion and sensation to 1st webspace

Common Peroneal Nerve Entrapment ❑Compression: ❑Common peroneal: (MC mononeuropathy in lower extremity): entrapment at the fibular head/neck due to extrinsic compression, stretch injury, direct trauma ❑Concerning presentation due to foot drop ❑Deep peroneal: entrapment at the ankle due to trauma, tight footwear, bone spur/scar tissue ❑Superficial peroneal nerve: entrapment in lateral compartment due to overstretching injuries or contusion ❑Treatment: Physical therapy, OMT, and avoidance of aggravating factors ❑Due to high conservative treatment success and appropriate identification, rarely is surgery required

RIB motion Bucket Handle Pump Handle Caliper not just inhalation and exhalation

Pump Handle From: Thorax Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8e, 2018 • This term is derived from an old fashioned water pump • One end is free, one end is fixed. The free end moves in an arc • This motion increases the ANTERIOR- POSTERIOR diameter of the ribcage • Ribs 2-5 have predominantly Pump Handle Motion

Bucket Handle From: Thorax Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8e, 2018 • The handle of a bucket is FIXED at both ends • Most excursion occurs through upward motion of its more LATERAL portion • This motion increases the TRANSVERSE diameter of the ribcage • Ribs 6-10 have predominantly Bucket Handle Motion

Caliper From: Anatomic Considerations of the Thoracic Cage An Osteopathic Approach to Diagnosis and Treatment, 3e, 2004 • This term is derived from an old-fashioned set of round calipers • No costotransverse articulations with the vertebra = less limitation of horizontal plane motion • This type of motion causes slight increases in both the ANTERIOR-POSTERIOR and TRANSVERSE diameters of the ribcage • Ribs 11-12 have predominantly Caliper Motion

• Characterized by spontaneous or evoked pain disproportionate in severity or duration to the inciting injury. • Pain does not follow a specific nerve territory or dermatomal distribution. • Distal predominance with abnormal sensory, motor, autonomic, and trophic findings. • Course is variable — symptoms may improve, stabilize, or worsen over time. Recognizing CRPS

EPIDEMIOLOGY • Population-based studies estimate an annual incidence of 5–26 per 100,000 person-years (Sandroni et al., 2003; de Mos et al., 2006) • CRPS is significantly more common in women, with a female-to-male ratio of approximately 3:1 to 4:1 • Peak incidence in women occurs between ages 61–70; median age of onset across studies is approximately 46 years

INCIDENCE ADULTS • ~75% female (F:M ratio 3:1–4:1) • Peak incidence ages 61–70; median onset ~46 yrs • Upper extremity most common (~60%) • Fracture most frequent precipitating event (~44%) CHILDREN • Rare; exact pediatric incidence unknown • Predominantly female (~75–90%); mean age ~12 yrs • Lower extremity affected in ~71–85% of cases • Generally better prognosis; recurrence is common

HISTORY Ambroise Paré — 16th century France • Royal surgeon to King Charles IX; first written account of a CRPS-like syndrome after limb phlebotomy (bloodletting) — described persistent burning pain and contractures Silas Weir Mitchell, MD — 1864 & 1872 • Union Army neurologist; observed severe burning pain in Civil War soldiers with partial nerve injuries — wounds healed but pain persisted • 1872: coined "causalgia" (Greek: kausos = burning heat + algos = pain) — pain grossly out of proportion to injury; skin "red and shining, as if varnished" • Published Injuries of Nerves and Their Consequences (1872) — foundational text establishing CRPS as a clinical entity distinct from simple nerve injury

HISTORY Paul Sudeck — 1900, Germany • Used X-ray to document post-traumatic bone atrophy — “Sudeck’s atrophy” — inflammatory demineralization visible on imaging within weeks of injury; one of the earliest objective findings in what we now call CRPS René Leriche — 1917 & 1939, France • 1917: first sympathectomy to relieve post-gunshot chronic hand pain — implicated the sympathetic nervous system as a driver of CRPS pain • 1939: proposed the “vicious cycle” hypothesis — tissue injury → abnormal SNS activation → vasoconstriction → more tissue ischemia → amplified pain (later shown to be an oversimplification) James A. Evans — 1946, USA → coined “RSD” • “Reflex Sympathetic Dystrophy” — dominated clinical usage for ~50 years but each word proved problematic: ◦ Reflex — pain arc is complex, multi-synaptic, not a simple reflex ◦ Sympathetic — many patients have no sympathetically maintained pain; SNS blockade often fails ◦ Dystrophy — tissue wasting is a late finding; rarely present in early or mild cases • Resulted in ~200 different names in the literature — massive diagnostic confusion and frequent mistreatment IASP Task Force — 1994: “RSD” officially retired → CRPS Type I & II introduced; Budapest criteria (2003) remain the diagnostic standard today

HISTORY • 1993: IASP convened a Task Force on Taxonomy to resolve the proliferation of inconsistent names for post-traumatic limb pain syndromes (~200 terms in the literature) • 1994: Consensus workshop in Orlando, FL — IASP officially retired "RSD" and introduced Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS); codified in the 2nd edition of Classification of Chronic Pain (Merskey & Bogduk) ◦ CRPS Type I — no confirmed nerve lesion (replaces RSD) ◦ CRPS Type II — confirmed peripheral nerve injury (replaces causalgia) • The name was chosen to be purely descriptive — deliberately avoiding any implication of etiopathology: ◦ Complex — multi-system involvement (sensory, autonomic, motor, trophic) ◦ Regional — confined to a body region, usually a distal extremity; not dermatomal ◦ Pain — the cardinal, required feature (disproportionate to the inciting event) ◦ Syndrome — a cluster of signs and symptoms, not a single-mechanism disease

PRECIPITATING CAUSES 42% Fractures (Colles' / distal radius most common) 21% Blunt trauma / sprains / soft tissue injury 12% Surgery (orthopedic, carpal tunnel, shoulder) 7% Carpal tunnel syndrome / nerve entrapment ~5% Spontaneous / no identifiable precipitant Also reported: immobilization, MI/CVA, venipuncture, minor procedures Source: Maihöfner et al., 2018 (n=1,043); de Mos et al., 2007; Sandroni et al., 2003

CLINICAL PRESENTATION • Onset within days to weeks of precipitating event (occasionally months) • Affects a distal extremity; pain is disproportionate to the inciting injury • Four symptom domains: Sensory • Vasomotor/Sudomotor • Motor • Trophic SENSORY • Severe burning or aching pain (continuous) • Allodynia (pain from light touch/clothing) • Hyperalgesia (exaggerated pain response) VASOMOTOR / SUDOMOTOR • Skin color changes (red, mottled, or pale) • Temperature asymmetry (>1°C vs. contralateral) • Edema; increased or decreased sweating MOTOR • Weakness, reduced range of motion • Tremor, dystonia, or myoclonus • Neglect-like phenomenon (ignoring limb) TROPHIC • Skin texture changes (shiny, thin, glossy) • Abnormal nail/hair growth; muscle atrophy • Osteoporosis (patchy bony demineralization)

PAIN PERCEPTION Where do we feel pain?

Copyrights apply NOCICEPTIVE PAIN 1) Noxious stimulus activates nociceptive terminals of primary sensory neurons 2) Action potentials (APs) are generated at the nociceptor 3) APs travel along Aδ- and C-fiber primary afferents toward the spinal cord 4) APs arrive at synapses in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord 5) Dorsal horn (Rexed laminae I, II, V) is the first central synapse in the pain pathway 6) Arriving APs open voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in presynaptic terminals

NOCICEPTIVE PAIN 7) Ca²⁺ influx triggers vesicle fusion → neurotransmitter release into the synaptic cleft 8) Glutamate and Substance P diffuse across cleft and bind to post-synaptic receptors (AMPA, NMDA, NK-1) 9) Receptor activation (via G-protein or ion channels) allows Na⁺ influx → depolarization of the post-synaptic dorsal horn neuron 10) New APs propagate up the spinothalamic tract → thalamus → somatosensory cortex (pain perception)

PERIPHERAL SENSITIZATION Tissue injury releases an “inflammatory soup” of mediators that lower nociceptor thresholds: • Bradykinin & prostaglandins — directly sensitize primary afferents; lower threshold to ATP, ACh, serotonin, mechanical and thermal stimuli • Substance P & CGRP — released retrogradely by afferents; trigger mast cell degranulation → histamine release → further afferent excitation (neurogenic inflammation) • Net result — sensitized afferents fire more frequently and at lower stimulus intensities → primary hyperalgesia and allodynia Peripheral sensitization drives the wind-up of central neurons seen in chronic CRPS

CENTRAL SENSITIZATION • Persistent afferent barrage lowers dorsal horn neuron threshold → neurons become hyperexcitable and transmit amplified APs for prolonged periods • Wind-up: repeated C-fiber input causes progressive amplification of dorsal horn responses via NMDA receptor activation • Receptor field expansion: dorsal horn neurons respond to inputs from adjacent areas → pain spreads beyond the original injury site (secondary hyperalgesia) • Loss of inhibition: reduced GABA/glycine interneuron activity removes normal descending inhibitory control • In CRPS: central sensitization persists long after the triggering injury has healed, sustaining chronic allodynia and hyperalgesia

NEUROPATHIC PAIN Pain arising from direct injury or dysfunction of the nervous system (PNS or CNS), without ongoing noxious stimulus • Nerve injury mechanisms: transection (complete or partial), compression, infiltration (infectious / inflammatory / ischemic) • Key features: spontaneous burning pain, allodynia, hyperalgesia, and dysesthesia in the distribution of the injured nerve • In CRPS: CRPS Type II (causalgia) involves confirmed nerve injury; Type I involves nerve dysfunction without identifiable lesion

NEUROPATHIC PAIN • ECTOPIC ACTIVITY – Nerve injury → Na⁺ channel accumulation at injury site → spontaneous APs fired without any stimulus • EPHAPTIC ACTIVITY – APs in damaged fibers “cross-talk” to adjacent unstimulated fibers via electrical coupling (no synapse) • EXPANDED RECEPTIVE FIELD – Ectopic + ephaptic activity cause pain to spread beyond the original nerve territory → explains diffuse CRPS pain

BUDAPEST CRITERIA (2003) 1) The presence of an initiating noxious event, or a cause of immobilization* 2) Continuing pain, allodynia, or hyperalgesia in which the pain is disproportionate to any known inciting event 3) Evidence at some time of edema, changes in skin blood flow or abnormal sudomotor activity in the region of pain. 4) This diagnosis is excluded by the existence of other conditions that would otherwise account for the degree of pain and dysfunction. *Not required for diagnosis as 5 - 10% of patients will not have this CRPS I –”RSD”= if seen without “major nerve damage” CRPS II –”Causalgia”= if seen in the presence of “major nerve damage”

Sympathetics • Visceral afferents are stimulated, leading to facilitated segments at T2-T7 and C2-C3 (parasympathetic) • Viscerosomatic reflexes occur producing palpable joint and musculoskeletal changes (somatic dysfunctions). • Prolonged sympathetic stimulation →vasoconstriction and local hypoperfusion.

Parasympathetics • The Hering-Breuer inflation reflex (reflex triggered to prevent over-inflation of the lung) cannot distinguish between air sacs filled with air and those filled with fluid • With lung tissue congestion →the respiratory center receives information from the Vagus nerve to limit excursion of the diaphragm. • At the same time, the carotid body signals the respiratory center that more oxygen is needed →an increase in the respiratory rate • The result is rapid, shallow breathing by the patient

Musculoskeletal component: • The diaphragm is mechanically stressed by: o Ribs and spine via viscerosomatic reflexes. o Tissue resistance due to congestion. o Don’t forget about the phrenic nerve innervation of the diaphragm… C3,4,5 keep the diaphragm alive! • This stress produces strain of the lower six ribs and thoracolumbar junction resulting in an increased lumbar lordosis and a flattening of the diaphragm. • T2-7 paraspinal tissues will have increased tone.
Lymphatics: • Flattening of the diaphragm results in decreased pressure gradient between thoracic and abdominal cavities → decreased lymph flow and increased tissue congestion
Pneumonia • Typical symptoms: o High fever o Tachypnea o Hypoxia o Chest pain, especially with deep inspiration o Cough

Pneumonia (Historical Context) • Spanish influenza outbreak in 1918 (viral condition that was frequently complicated by superimposed bacterial pneumonia) o First time that statistical records kept of OMT vs. standard medical care • Antibiotics not available • 100,000 patient received osteopathic manipulation while being treated for the influenza →0.25% mortality rate • Standard medical care at the time →estimated 5% overall mortality rate • Patients with superimposed bacterial pneumonia: o Medically treated: 30-60% mortality rate o Received osteopathic care: 10% mortality rate

General Goals of Osteopathic Treatment in Respiratory Infections 1. Improve venous and lymphatic flow 2. Improve arterial circulation to carry immune system products to the lungs 3. Ease removal of accumulated bronchial secretions and phlegm 4. Decrease workload of breathing

Pneumonia Goals of treatment: • Decrease congestion • Decrease sympathetic hyperactivity o Areas of hypersympathetic activity should be treated first o These areas enhanced by facilitated segments related to the sympathetic innervation for the affected organ o Facilitation results from excessive visceral afferent impulses originating from the irritated lung tissue • Decrease mechanical impediments to thoracic cage motion

Pneumonia OMT for pneumonia: • Encourages the removal of waste products • Reduces vascular constriction • Enhances medical therapy • Improves respiration • Makes the patient more comfortable and supports the patient’s own self-healing and protective mechanisms • Manipulation works synergistically with the medical treatment directed toward the disease process

Pneumonia Specific OMT: • Treatment of sympathetic VSRs o Rib raising techniques – how long? o Paraspinal inhibition o Chapman points • Lymphatic techniques o Pump techniques contraindicated in acute phase while patient is febrile o Helps improve immunity and drug delivery to tissues o Remember to open the thoracic inlet first!

Pneumonia Multicenter Osteopathic Pneumonia Study in the Elderly (MOPSE) trial: • 406 subjects aged ≥50 years hospitalized with pneumonia at 7 community hospitals • Significant reductions between OMT vs conventional care in the following parameters • Length of stay • Duration of IV antibiotics • Respiratory failure resulting in ventilator use • Death
